'''''Bernstein v. United States''''' was a series of court cases filed by [[Daniel J. Bernstein]], then a mathematics Ph.D. student at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], challenging U.S. government restrictions on the [[Export of cryptography from the United States|export of cryptographic software]]. In the early 1990s, the U.S. government classified encryption software as a "munition," imposing strict export controls. As a result, Bernstein was required to register as an arms dealer and obtain an export license before he could publish his encryption software online.

With the support of the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation|Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF)]], Bernstein filed a lawsuit against the U.S. government, arguing that the export controls violated his [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] rights. The case ultimately led to a relaxation of export restrictions on cryptography, which facilitated the development of secure international e-commerce. The decision has been recognized by First Amendment and technology advocacy groups for affirming a "[[Code as speech|right to code]]" and applying First Amendment protections to code as a [[Freedom of expression|form of expression]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dame-Boyle |first=Alison |date=2015-04-16 |title=EFF at 25: Remembering the Case that Established Code as Speech |url=https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2015/04/remembering-case-established-code-speech |access-date=2024-11-08 |website=Electronic Frontier Foundation |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Bernstein v. United States Department of States (District Court of California) (1997) |url=https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/bernstein-v-united-states-department-of-states-district-court-of-california/ |access-date=2024-11-08 |website=The Free Speech Center |language=en-US}}</ref>

==History==
The case was first brought in 1995, when Bernstein was a student at [[University of California, Berkeley]], and wanted to publish a paper and associated [[source code]] on his '''''Snuffle''''' encryption system. Bernstein was represented by the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation]], who hired outside lawyer [[Cindy Cohn]] and also obtained ''[[Pro bono|pro bono publico]]'' assistance from Lee Tien of Berkeley; M. Edward Ross of the San Francisco law firm of Steefel, Levitt & Weiss; James Wheaton and Elizabeth Pritzker of the First Amendment Project in Oakland; and Robert Corn-Revere, Julia Kogan, and Jeremy Miller of the Washington, D.C., law firm of Hogan & Hartson. After four years and one regulatory change, the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit|Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals]] ruled that [[software]] [[source code]] was speech protected by the [[First Amendment to the United States Constitution|First Amendment]] and that the government's regulations preventing its publication were unconstitutional.<ref>{{cite web
| url=https://www.epic.org/crypto/export_controls/bernstein_decision_9_cir.html
| title=U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit: Bernstein v. USDOJ
| date=1999-05-06
| publisher=[[Electronic Privacy Information Center]]
| accessdate=2019-04-17}}</ref>  Regarding those regulations, the [[Electronic Frontier Foundation|EFF]] states:
{{blockquote|text=Years before, the government had placed encryption, a method for scrambling messages so they can only be understood by their intended recipients, on the [[United States Munitions List]], alongside bombs and [[flamethrower]]s, as a weapon to be regulated for national security purposes. Companies and individuals exporting items on the munitions list, including software with encryption capabilities, had to obtain prior [[United States Department of State|State Department]] approval.|author=Electronic Frontier Foundation: ''EFF's History''<ref name=EFF_History>{{cite web|url=https://www.eff.org/about/history|title=EFF's History|date=7 October 2011 |publisher=[[Electronic Frontier Foundation]]|accessdate=4 May 2012}}</ref>}}

The government requested ''[[en banc]]'' review.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Bernstein|first1=Daniel J.|title=Summary of the case status|url=https://cr.yp.to/export/status.html|website=cr.yp.to|accessdate=2019-04-17}}</ref> In ''Bernstein v. U.S. Dept. of Justice'', 192 F.3d 1308 (9th Cir. 1999), the Ninth Circuit ordered that this case be reheard by the ''en banc'' court, and withdrew the three-judge panel opinion, ''Bernstein v. U.S. Dept. of Justice'', 176 F.3d 1132 (9th Cir. 1999).<ref>{{cite journal|title=192 F. 3d 1308 – Daniel Bernstein v. United States Department of Justice|url=https://openjurist.org/192/f3d/1308/daniel-bernstein-v-united-states-department-of-justice|website=OpenJurist|year=1999 |volume=F3d |issue=192 |page=1308 |accessdate=2019-04-17}}</ref>

The government modified the regulations again,{{when|date=January 2025}} substantially loosening them, and Bernstein, then a professor at the [[University of Illinois Chicago]], challenged them again. This time, he chose to represent himself, although he had no formal legal training. On October 15, 2003, almost nine years after Bernstein first brought the case, the judge dismissed it and asked Bernstein to come back when the government made a "concrete threat".<ref>{{cite web|last1=Bernstein|first1=Daniel J.|title=Press Release: Crypto Case on indefinite hold|url=https://cr.yp.to/export/2003/10.15-bernstein.txt|website=cr.yp.to|accessdate=2019-04-17}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
Apple cited ''Bernstein v. US'' in its [[Apple–FBI encryption dispute|refusal to hack the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone]], arguing that they could not be compelled to "speak" (write code).<ref>{{cite magazine|author1=Kim Zetter|author2=Brian Barrett |title=Apple to FBI: You Can't Force Us to Hack the San Bernardino iPhone|magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/2016/02/apple-brief-fbi-response-iphone/ |date=February 25, 2016 |accessdate=2021-01-06}}</ref>

In 2022, Bernstein filed a second lawsuit against the U.S. government under the [[Freedom of Information Act (United States)|Freedom of Information Act]], seeking records on the [[National Security Agency]]'s role in influencing [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NIST]]'s [[post-quantum cryptography]] standards, a case that remains ongoing as of 2025.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blog.cr.yp.to/20220805-nsa.html|title=NSA, NIST, and post-quantum cryptography|last=Bernstein|first=Daniel J.|date=August 5, 2022|website=The cr.yp.to blog|access-date=November 24, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://nist.pqcrypto.org/foia/index.html|title=NSA-NIST-PQC FOIA responses|last=Bernstein|first=Daniel J.|date=2025|website=Post-quantum cryptography|access-date=November 24, 2025}}</ref>
